title: 5 GitHub Actions Alternatives for Frontend Teams
summary: Compare five GitHub Actions alternatives for frontend teams, including CircleCI, Buildkite, Jenkins, Woodpecker CI and Dagger, with setup examples and guidance.
body_markdown:
The strongest GitHub Actions alternatives for frontend teams are CircleCI for fully hosted CI, Buildkite for a hosted control plane running on hosted or self-hosted agents, Jenkins and Woodpecker CI for fully self-hosted CI, and Dagger for pipelines as code that run the same way on a laptop and in any CI.


The usual trigger is a bill full of runner minutes, a pull request waiting in a queue, or a workflow that only fails on GitHub’s runners and never on your machine. This article assumes you already know the[GitHub Actions workflow model](https://blog.openreplay.com/a-practical-guide-to-github-actions/) . It compares five options on the same three points: who each one suits, where its jobs run, and what an install, lint, test and build job looks like for a Node frontend.


## Key Takeaways


- If every CI job only calls` npm ci` ,` npm run lint` ,` npm test` and` npm run build` , switching CI tools means rewriting a few lines of YAML, not the pipeline’s logic.
- Buildkite hosts the orchestration while jobs run on agents: Buildkite-hosted Linux, Buildkite-hosted macOS on paid plans, or machines your team runs.
- CircleCI is hosted CI configured in` .circleci/config.yml` , and it supports self-hosted runners on every plan, including Free.
- Jenkins and Woodpecker are self-hosted. You stop paying per minute and start paying for servers and upkeep.
- Dagger is not a CI service. It is pipeline code that runs locally and inside whatever CI you already use.


## Why Do Frontend Teams Look for GitHub Actions Alternatives?


Frontend teams usually leave GitHub Actions for one of four reasons: hosted runner minutes cost too much, hosted runners sit in a queue, they need to run agents on their own hardware, or they can’t reproduce a[CI/CD pipeline](https://blog.openreplay.com/what-is-a-ci-cd-pipeline/) locally. Check the second reason before you migrate. If queued hosted runners are your only problem,[GitHub Actions self-hosted runners](https://docs.github.com/en/actions/hosting-your-own-runners/managing-self-hosted-runners/about-self-hosted-runners) may fix it without changing tools. GitLab CI/CD is mainly worth considering if you would also move your repositories, and its setup is covered in[GitLab CI/CD pipelines](https://blog.openreplay.com/gitlab-ci-cd-pipelines/) .


To keep the comparison fair, put the build logic in` package.json` so that every CI tool calls the same scripts:


```text
{
"  scripts  "  : {
"  lint  "  :   "  eslint .  "  ,
"  test  "  :   "  vitest run  "  ,
"  build  "  :   "  vite build  "
}
}
```


Swap in your framework’s own commands. In each example below, the CI configuration does only one job: it runs` npm ci` and then these three scripts.


## Buildkite


Buildkite suits teams that want hosted orchestration but need control over the machines that run their jobs. Buildkite supports both models: agents you run yourself, and agents Buildkite hosts for you.[Buildkite-hosted Linux agents](https://buildkite.com/docs/agent/buildkite-hosted/linux) are available on every plan, including Free, which is limited to the small machine size.[Buildkite-hosted macOS agents](https://buildkite.com/docs/agent/buildkite-hosted/macos) require a Pro or Enterprise plan. Self-hosted agents[poll Buildkite for work](https://github.com/buildkite/agent) , so you don’t have to open any inbound ports. Buildkite offers a free account to start.


```text
# .buildkite/pipeline.yml
steps  :
-   label  :   "  Install, lint, test, build  "
commands  :
-   npm ci
-   npm run lint
-   npm test
-   npm run build
plugins  :
-   docker#v5.14.0  :
image  :   "  node:<your-node-version>  "
```


The[Docker plugin](https://github.com/buildkite-plugins/docker-buildkite-plugin/releases) runs the commands inside a Node image, so the agent only needs Docker. If Node is already installed on the agent, you can drop the` plugins` block.


**Verdict:** Buildkite is the best fit when you want to own your compute without running a CI server. The trade-off is that you manage the agent fleet unless you use hosted agents.


## CircleCI


CircleCI suits teams that want a fully hosted service with minimal infrastructure. CircleCI is hosted first, and it also offers[self-hosted runners on all plans](https://circleci.com/docs/guides/execution-runner/runner-overview/) , including Free. By default, your code runs on CircleCI’s infrastructure. CircleCI’s[configuration introduction](https://circleci.com/docs/guides/getting-started/config-intro/) identifies 2.1 as the most recent version.


```text
# .circleci/config.yml
version  :   2.1


jobs  :
build  :
docker  :
-   image  :   cimg/node:<full.node.version>
steps  :
-   checkout
-   run  :   npm ci
-   run  :   npm run lint
-   run  :   npm test
-   run  :   npm run build


workflows  :
ci  :
jobs  :
-   build
```


Pin[cimg/node](https://circleci.com/developer/images/image/cimg/node) to your project’s full Node version. CircleCI also supports dependency caching, but it is left out here to keep the example short. YAML mistakes are a common reason a first CircleCI push fails, so it’s worth running the file through the[OpenReplay YAML validator](https://openreplay.com/tools/yaml-validator/) to catch syntax errors before you commit.


**Verdict:** CircleCI is the closest like-for-like replacement for GitHub Actions. It makes sense if minutes and queues are the problem but you still don’t want to run servers.


## Jenkins


Jenkins suits teams with strict on-premises requirements and someone who has time to maintain it. Jenkins is self-hosted only. The software is free and open source, but the cost moves from per-minute billing to the servers, plugins and upgrades your team maintains. Pipelines live in a` Jenkinsfile` written in[declarative Pipeline syntax](https://www.jenkins.io/doc/book/pipeline/syntax/) :


```text
pipeline {
agent any
stages {
stage(  '  Install  '  ) { steps { sh   '  npm ci  '   } }
stage(  '  Lint  '  )    { steps { sh   '  npm run lint  '   } }
stage(  '  Test  '  )    { steps { sh   '  npm test  '   } }
stage(  '  Build  '  )   { steps { sh   '  npm run build  '   } }
}
}
```


` agent any` assumes that Node is installed on whichever agent picks up the job.


**Verdict:** pick Jenkins only when self-hosting is a hard requirement. For most frontend teams, the upkeep costs more than the minutes it saves.


## Woodpecker CI


Woodpecker CI suits small teams that want lightweight, self-hosted CI with YAML that feels familiar. Woodpecker CI is self-hosted, and every step runs its commands inside the container named in the step, as set out in the[workflow syntax](https://woodpecker-ci.org/docs/usage/workflow-syntax) . Workflows can go in a[.woodpecker/ directory](https://woodpecker-ci.org/docs/usage/workflows) , with one workflow per file.


```text
# .woodpecker/ci.yaml
steps  :
-   name  :   install
image  :   node:<your-node-version>
commands  :
-   npm ci
-   name  :   lint
image  :   node:<your-node-version>
commands  :
-   npm run lint
-   name  :   test
image  :   node:<your-node-version>
commands  :
-   npm test
-   name  :   build
image  :   node:<your-node-version>
commands  :
-   npm run build
```


Splitting the work into four steps doesn’t mean installing four times. Steps run in sequence by default, and the checked-out workspace is mounted into every step, so the` node_modules` folder from` install` is still there in` build` . With woodpecker-cli and a supported backend installed, you can[run a workflow locally](https://woodpecker-ci.org/docs/usage/local-execution) with` woodpecker-cli exec` before pushing it.


**Verdict:** for self-hosting, Woodpecker CI is a simpler choice than Jenkins. The downside is that you run the server and the agents yourself.


## Dagger: Pipelines as Code, Not a CI Service


Dagger is not a hosted CI service, and it doesn’t replace one. You write the pipeline as code with a Dagger SDK, and the same code runs on a laptop and inside any CI system, GitHub Actions included. The[SDK docs](https://docs.dagger.io/reference/sdks/) cover Go, Python, TypeScript, Java, PHP and Elixir, plus Dang, Dagger’s own scripting language. Here is the same job in TypeScript, using a module created with` dagger init --sdk=typescript --name=frontend-ci` :


```text
import   {   dag  ,   Directory  ,   object  ,   func   }   from   "  @dagger.io/dagger  "


@  object  ()
class   FrontendCi   {
@  func  ()
async   check  (  source  :   Directory  ,   nodeVersion  :   string  )  :   Promise  <  string  > {
return   await   dag
.  container  ()
.  from  (  `  node:  ${  nodeVersion  }`  )
.  withMountedDirectory  (  "  /src  "  ,   source  )
.  withWorkdir  (  "  /src  "  )
.  withExec  ([  "  npm  "  ,   "  ci  "  ])
.  withExec  ([  "  npm  "  ,   "  run  "  ,   "  lint  "  ])
.  withExec  ([  "  npm  "  ,   "  test  "  ])
.  withExec  ([  "  npm  "  ,   "  run  "  ,   "  build  "  ])
.  stdout  ()
}
}
```


Run it locally with` dagger call check --source=. --node-version=<your-node-version>` . Your existing CI job then runs that same command and nothing else. If a local run passes, the CI run executes the identical container steps. The cost is one more SDK and engine for the team to learn.


These commands are for Dagger 0.x.[Dagger 1.0](https://dagger.io/blog/dagger-10-beta/) , announced in beta in October 2026, renames them:` dagger module init` creates a module, and` dagger call` becomes` dagger api call` . The TypeScript code itself stays the same.


## How Do You Choose a GitHub Actions Alternative?


The right GitHub Actions alternative depends on where you want jobs to run:


- **If you want fully hosted CI with nothing to operate,** use CircleCI. Its config maps closely to what you already have.
- **If you want hosted orchestration on your own or vendor-hosted machines,** use Buildkite, especially if you need macOS builds.
- **If self-hosting is required and you have the people to maintain it,** use Jenkins.
- **If self-hosting is required and you want something small,** use Woodpecker CI.
- **If the real problem is “works locally, fails in CI”,** add Dagger, and keep any of the tools above, or GitHub Actions itself, as the runner.
- **If the only problem is queue time,** try GitHub Actions self-hosted runners first.


Woodpecker’s Docker backend and Dagger both need a container runtime. If Docker Desktop doesn’t suit your machines, Dagger also runs on Podman and nerdctl, and Woodpecker can run on Kubernetes or straight on the host with its local backend.


Whichever tool you pick, start by moving all build logic into npm scripts. Then trial the replacement on a single branch, running in parallel with GitHub Actions, and compare the results for a week before you switch over.


## FAQs


Does GitHub charge per minute for self-hosted runners in GitHub Actions?


No. GitHub does not bill per-minute fees for self-hosted runner usage, so the cost is the machines you run them on. In December 2025, GitHub announced a platform charge of 0.002 US dollars per minute for self-hosted runners from March 1, 2026, then postponed it to re-evaluate its approach. Check GitHub's Actions billing documentation before building a cost comparison on either figure.


Can I run a CircleCI job locally before pushing it?


Yes, one job at a time. The CircleCI CLI runs a single job inside Docker on your machine with circleci local execute. Workflows do not run locally, and the machine executor is not supported. For a version 2.1 config, first export the processed config with circleci config process, then pass that file to circleci local execute using the -c flag and the job name.


Does Woodpecker CI work with repositories hosted on GitHub?


Yes. Woodpecker supports GitHub, including GitHub Enterprise, as well as GitLab, Gitea, Forgejo and Bitbucket Cloud. You register an OAuth application on the forge and pass its client ID and secret to the Woodpecker server through environment variables such as WOODPECKER_GITHUB_CLIENT and WOODPECKER_GITHUB_SECRET. Repositories stay on GitHub, Woodpecker reports pipeline status back to it, and only the server and agents run on your infrastructure.


How do I run a Dagger function from an existing GitHub Actions workflow?


Add a step that uses the official dagger/dagger-for-github action after actions/checkout. The action installs the Dagger CLI, starts a Dagger Engine on the runner and calls your function. Set verb to call and pass the same arguments you use locally, such as check with your source directory and Node version. The pipeline logic stays in the module, so leaving GitHub Actions later only changes this thin wrapper.
